The Paradox of Thrift: When Everyone Saves, No One Does

In micro, a household that tightens its belt really does save more. In macro, when every household tightens at once, the story flips.

When everyone closes their wallet, 🏪 shops sell less. When shops sell less, 🧑 workers earn less. And when income falls, there is less 💰 money left to save. The plan to save ends up blocking saving itself. What is true for one household turns false for all of them together.

For example, say all 30 classmates stop visiting the snack bar to save their allowances. The owner earns nothing and cuts orders from the supply shop. The supply shop struggles too. The classmates filled their 🐷 piggy banks, but the neighborhood as a whole saved no more than before.

Examples & Exercises

Counterexample

Fearing a downturn, every household cuts its spending by 444 to save more. Investment is fixed.

How much does the whole economy's saving rise?

Verdict

The claim is false — even though every household cuts spending to save more, the economy's realized saving stays at 303030, not a won more

Show proof

Counterexample and verification

  1. When spending falls, shop incomes fall, and the smaller incomes cut spending again. Through the multiplier, income drops by 41−0.8=20\frac{4}{1 - 0.8} = 201−0.84​=20, from 210210210 to 190190190.

  2. At the old income of 210210210 they planned to raise saving from 303030 to 343434.

    But income fell to 190190190, and realized saving is 303030 — investment 202020 plus the government deficit 101010 — exactly where it started.

    Not a won more.

Now take an economy where investment moves with income (I=20+0.1YI = 20 + 0.1YI=20+0.1Y; income is currently 420420420).

What happens to saving under the same thrift shock of 444?

Show proof

  1. Now the multiplier is 11−0.8−0.1=10\frac{1}{1 - 0.8 - 0.1} = 101−0.8−0.11​=10, so income falls by 404040, from 420420420 to 380380380, and as sales shrink, firms cut investment from 626262 to 585858.

  2. Realized saving moves with investment, sliding from 727272 to 686868. Everyone tried to save 444 more — and the economy as a whole saved 444 less.
